go nuts

Eating out with a nut allergy, without the guesswork

An agent team that reads restaurants' real menus, rates every dish for peanut and tree-nut risk with the menu's own words as evidence, and helps diners call ahead.

Elise Lehman · MGT 409 · AI Foundations for Managers · Yale SOM · Fall 2026 · October 2026
Live app: go-nuts-mepgzkf6appmyn8z3rqm8ts.streamlit.app
GitHub: github.com/elehman28/go-nuts
Demo video (57 s, narrated): report/go-nuts-demo.mp4
Model: gpt-6-luna via Portkey (the only model on the course key). All numbers in this report are computed from the app's own database and usage log (2026-10-19 to 2026-10-20).

89restaurant menus checked

1. Motivation

I have a nut allergy, and so do some members of my family. For us, going out to eat starts long before we sit down: someone has to find the restaurant's menu, read every description for peanuts and tree nuts, guess at the sauces and desserts that don't say what is in them, and call ahead with questions. The result is that dinner with people we love is often spent thinking about what is on the plate instead of who is at the table.

Go Nuts gives us reassurance before we get to the restaurant, so we can focus on spending time with each other rather than on whether something contains nuts. It does not promise safety. It makes the homework faster, more thorough and more consistent, and it tells you exactly what to ask the server.

The problem is common and serious. In a nationally representative survey, 10.8% of US adults had a convincing food allergy, 1.8% to peanut and 1.2% to tree nuts; 51.1% of adults with a food allergy had had a severe reaction and 38.3% had visited an emergency department for one at some point [1]. Among US children, 7.6% have a food allergy (peanut 2.2%, tree nut 1.2%) [2]. Restaurants are a known weak point: in a CDC study of 278 restaurants, only 44.4% of managers, 40.8% of food workers and 33.3% of servers had received any food-allergy training [3], and in US registry data 28% of food-allergy deaths (18 of 63) were linked to food from restaurants or other food establishments [4].

2. What is new

Existing tools help in pieces. None of the nine options we reviewed reads a restaurant's actual menu dish by dish and rates each dish for nut risk with the menu's own words as evidence (research notes in report/research-notes.md; items we could not confirm are marked).

OptionWhat it doesReads real menus dish by dish?Translated chef cards?
AllergyEats [5]Diners rate how well restaurants handled their allergyNo: ratings, not menu analysisNot confirmed
Spokin [6]Community reviews filtered by allergyNo: reviewsNot confirmed
Fig (Food Is Good) [7]Scans packaged-food barcodes; lists some chain restaurant optionsPartly: chains onlyNot confirmed
Equal Eats [8]Allergy translation cards (paid tiers)NoYes (about 50 languages claimed)
SelectWisely [9]Printed or PDF allergy translation cardsNoYes (40+ languages)
MenuTrinfo / AllerTrain [10]Paid allergen analysis and staff training for restaurantsFor paying restaurants, not dinersNo
Nima sensor [11]Portable test of one food sampleNo (one sample at a time); peanut sensor reportedly discontinuedNo
FARE chef card templateFill-in allergy card for restaurantsNoNot confirmed
Yelp / Google reviewsGeneral reviewsNoNo
Go NutsReads the real menu, rates every dish with a quote, ranks restaurants for your profile, gives the phone number to callYesYes: 6 languages, from your profile

Go Nuts is also new in how it treats the AI. The model is never trusted on its own: every rating must quote the menu, and a plain-code Verifier checks every quote against the page, re-scans the whole menu for nut words and known hidden sources (pesto, praline, marzipan, almond milk, cashew vegan cheese), and can only raise a dish's risk, never lower it. Nothing is ever called "safe": the best rating is "No nuts listed, still ask staff".

3. Agent design

Go Nuts is a team of seven agents that talk through a shared message bus. Any agent can hand a task to any other, and the bus records every hand-off for the Agent trace and stops runaway delegation (no loops, at most 8 levels deep and 60 hand-offs per request). Four agents use the model, and only when they must; the other three are plain code, which makes them free, fast and predictable.

AgentRoleToolsModel?
FinderTurns a place (or "Near me") into nearby restaurants with phone numbers and addressesOpenStreetMap (Overpass, four mirrors with caching), reverse address lookupNo
Menu FetcherGets menu text: web pages and linked menu pages, PDFs, GoNation menu data, chains' official allergen charts; menu photosHTTP with private-address blocking, PDF reader, character-position chart reader, image readerPhotos only
Menu AnalystRates every dish (contains / likely / unclear / no nuts listed) with a word-for-word quote and a reason; notes the kitchen's allergy statementsdelegate tool (any teammate)Yes
VerifierRemoves prompt-injection lines before the AI sees a menu; checks quotes; flags hidden nuts; screens community posts and photos for personal informationText matching, hidden-nut list (seeded plus community warnings)No
SummarizerRanks restaurants for the diner's profile; writes a short verdict and questions for the serverdelegate toolYes
Cost ControlCaches every analysis by restaurant and by menu text; enforces session (150K) and daily (2M) token budgetsSQLiteNo
Food GuideAnswers chat questions ("I just ate pad thai, are there usually nuts in it?", "What could I order at September in Bangkok?"). Plain code first finds the restaurants named (typos allowed) and real counts from checked menus ("pad thai": 9 of 11 listings contain nuts); one model call writes the answer; the Verifier checks itSummarizer (saved dish ratings), Verifier, Cost ControlYes

Model choice. The course key allows only gpt-6-luna, so the design question was how to use it well. It reads photos (tested on a tilted, blurred menu photo: every dish, nut and price correct; one misspelling), follows a strict JSON format, and is inexpensive. Two real-model findings shaped the design: big menus were cut off because hidden reasoning counts toward the output limit, so the Analyst reads menus in 4,000-character pieces with reasoning turned off (measured below), and one call stalled for over six minutes, so every call now has a 90-second timeout.

One real run, step by step

Below is a real request on the live model (not a mock), traced by the app. The input was a made-up test menu ("Harbor Grill", not a real restaurant) that hides two lines telling the AI to mark every dish nut-free, plus two ordinary dishes so the menu text was new and not answered from the cache.

  1. You → Summarizer (check_menu): the diner's profile is peanuts and all tree nuts, severe.
  2. Summarizer → Cost Control (get_menu_report): no saved result for this exact menu text, so a fresh analysis is needed.
  3. Cost Control → Menu Analyst (analyze_menu).
  4. Menu Analyst → Verifier (screen_text): both injection lines are removed before the model sees the menu. Plain code, 0 tokens.
  5. The Analyst calls gpt-6-luna: 1,703 input tokens, 1,564 of them served from the prompt cache, 586 output, 6.3 s.
  6. Menu Analyst → Verifier (verify_analysis): every quote is found on the menu; no dish lowered; nut words re-scanned.
  7. Summarizer writes the verdict and server questions (1,127 in, 223 out, 3.4 s); Cost Control saves both so the next diner pays nothing. Total: 7 hand-offs, 3,639 tokens, 9.7 seconds.

Cost at scale

The one assumption here is marked: a diner looks up 8 restaurants a month (assumption, not measured). Everything else is measured: today's cache hit rate, the mean fresh-check cost and the mean summary cost.

ScenarioMonthly cost
Per restaurant lookup (blended at today's 73% cache hit rate)$0.00083
Per user per month (8 lookups)$0.0067
100 users$0.67
10,000 users$66.63
Keeping the whole city fresh (re-read all 89 checked menus every 14 days), independent of users$0.43

The key property: cost grows with the number of restaurants, not the number of diners. New Haven has a few hundred restaurants; once a menu is checked, every diner shares the saved analysis and pays only for a short personalized summary (also cached per profile). With 10,000 users the real hit rate would be far above today's 73%, so the 10,000-user line above is an upper bound. The course key's 2M-token daily cap allows about 435 fresh menu checks a day.

Cost cuts and their measured trade-offs

  • Two-level cache (by restaurant, and by menu text, so two restaurants with the same menu share one analysis): 73% hit rate, 5,012,794 tokens saved.
  • Prompt caching: 30% of all input tokens were served from the provider's cache because every Analyst prompt starts with the same instructions; in the traced run, 1,564 of 1,703 input tokens.
  • Reasoning off for the Analyst. Measured on one real 5,958-character menu piece: default reasoning used 5,493 output tokens (2,133 of them hidden reasoning) in 39.6 s; reasoning off used 3,248 tokens in 24.6 s with a similar answer (41% fewer output tokens, 38% faster). Trade-off: the model thinks less, so the plain-code Verifier's nut re-scan is the backstop, and it can only raise risk.
  • Menus in 4,000-character pieces. Before this, five large menus failed because answers were cut off; after it, all finished (Claire's Corner Copia 79 dishes, Costa Pizza 171, Barcelona 127). Trade-off: more calls per big menu, but no wasted half-answers.
  • Plain code wherever possible: GoNation menu data, Domino's allergen chart and Chipotle's allergen statement are read with 0 tokens; sites with almost no text fail fast without a model call; sites that failed are skipped for 14 days (65 skipped in the latest scan).

5. Safety

Three kinds of risk, each with a built defense, and evidence that the defense works. The app ships with 90 automated tests (fake model, free to run: pytest).

Attacks

  • Prompt injection in menus. Menu text is data, never instructions. The Verifier removes lines that address the AI before the model sees them, and anything the model still finds suspicious is reported. Shown working in the screenshot in section 3: both hidden lines were removed and the nut dishes were still flagged.
  • Malicious web content. Restaurant pages are untrusted. We found and fixed two real holes during testing: dish names and quotes from websites were being placed into the page as raw HTML (now escaped), and a javascript: address in a restaurant's map record could have become a clickable link (now only web, phone and map links are allowed). Both have tests. Two New Haven restaurant domains had become spam or gambling sites; the Fetcher follows only the restaurant's own site, so it never followed their links.
  • Private addresses. The Fetcher refuses links to private or local network addresses, so a pasted link cannot make the server attack itself.

Agent malfunction

  • Invented or misquoted dishes: every rating needs a word-for-word quote; unverifiable dishes are sent back to the Analyst once and dropped if they aren't on the menu.
  • Cut-off or garbled answers are detected (finish reason, JSON check) and retried in halves at most once, then reported in plain words.
  • Misreading charts. Domino's allergen PDF loses its columns as plain text, so we read each mark by its position. A first version counted only check marks and would have shown no nut risk at all; the chart's second symbol (■, "manufactured in a facility that handles peanuts and tree nuts") marks two desserts, which are now flagged.
  • Chat answers are checked in plain code before they are shown: every dish the Food Guide says a restaurant serves must be on that restaurant's saved menu (otherwise it is flagged as unconfirmed), "safe" and "nut-free" claims are reworded, and when someone says they already ate something or describes symptoms, the answer always starts with the same emergency steps (use epinephrine if prescribed, call 911). Tested with real questions, including one with a typo in the restaurant's name.
  • Partial menus (fewer than 10 dishes, or a chain's store page) are labeled, listed last, and never shown green.
  • Honest labels: AI-written text, AI inferences and official chain data are each tagged; diner photos and sample menus are labeled; approximate addresses say so. In one check, 9 map-based addresses were corrected by the restaurants' own websites, including one that was off by about 1,000 street numbers.

Overspending

  • Session budget 150K tokens and app-wide daily budget 2M tokens (tested); a 90-second timeout per call; caps on every loop (pieces per menu, retries, menu links, photos, delegation hops). Large scans needed the student's approval in advance (about 800K tokens approved, about 720K used).

Privacy

  • No accounts. The allergy profile and saved list stay in a cookie on the diner's device, only if they tick "Remember". "Near me" rounds location to about 100 m and never stores it. Reviews and feedback reject emails, phone numbers, addresses and handles; community photos are screened by the model and rejected if a person or personal information is visible (fails closed); photo location data is stripped; menu photos are never stored. Feedback is anonymous and saved only with consent.

6. Impact

What Go Nuts has done so far, all measured from its database:

  • 89 New Haven-area menus checked (73 full, 16 partial), 5,940 dishes rated: 275 contain nuts, 101 likely contain nuts, 3,170 unclear (ask staff), 2,394 with no nuts listed. 53% are "unclear", which is the honest answer when a menu leaves ingredients out; each comes with a question to ask.
  • 380 restaurants on the map, every one with an address (42 from the restaurant's own website, the rest from OpenStreetMap, labeled approximate where estimated) and 134 with a phone number to call ahead.
  • Hidden nuts surfaced that a quick read would miss: a Thai iced tea made with Frangelico (a hazelnut liqueur) and fried chicken breaded with almond milk at September in Bangkok; peanut in that restaurant's tom yum soup and mango sticky rice; two Domino's desserts made in a facility with peanuts and tree nuts.
  • Speed: a fresh menu check takes 8.5 s of model time (median); a restaurant someone has already checked is instant.
  • Allergy chef card in English, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Chinese and Arabic, made from the diner's profile, a first step toward international travel. Interviews with adults with peanut and tree-nut allergies found foreign travel especially hard, with translated allergy cards a common coping strategy [12].

First users

Three people with nut allergies tried Go Nuts in October 2026: me, through the in-app feedback form, and two testers whose answers I collected directly. All three are anonymous here, and both testers agreed to be quoted. Each estimated how long it takes to check one restaurant's menu for nuts.

7. Limits and next steps

  • Coverage. 89 restaurant websites could not be read: 54 have no menu text (JavaScript-only menus, pictures, or ordering apps like Toast and Menufy that need private keys) and 35 were down, gone, or blocking readers. Many restaurants list no website at all. Diners can add any menu by photo from the Map.
  • Chains. Most national chains' allergen guides load through apps or block downloads; Go Nuts links to each chain's official guide and reads Domino's and Chipotle with plain code.
  • AI accuracy. Ratings are AI-assisted and checked against the menu text, but menus omit ingredients and kitchens change recipes; Go Nuts cannot see cross-contact. Accuracy has not yet been measured against human-labeled menus.
  • Data quality. Some addresses are approximate (from the map location), and the chef card translations were written carefully but not by native speakers; the app says so.
  • Hosting. Reviews, photos and feedback live in the hosted app's database and reset if it restarts; the course key's daily token cap limits fresh checks per day.

Next steps: (1) a larger user trial through the feedback form, with timed rather than estimated minutes; (2) an Accuracy Auditor that compares ratings with menus labeled by hand; (3) a Menu Watcher that re-checks only menus that changed; (4) more cities; (5) international travel, our family's real hope: menus in other languages and chef cards for any destination.
